title: Downtime conversation kit for customer-facing teams
content:
Purpose:
This kit gives account, sales, CSM and support teams short, medium and long-form language for talking to customers during latency or availability incidents affecting inference: what happened, how Redwood mitigates impact, what customers can expect, and why Redwood’s approach preserves trust and business continuity.

Audience:
- Account execs and sales engineers preparing for customer check-ins during incidents
- CSMs and support responding to inbound customer concerns
- GTM content writers who need plug-and-play snippets

Top-line positioning (one-line):
Redwood minimizes customer impact during service stress by routing, automatic fallbacks, and predictable degradation controls so applications stay usable and recover gracefully.

Key messages by timeframe
- Immediate (first contact):
  - Simple: “We’re seeing elevated latency for model endpoints in X region. Our system has automatically routed traffic to a healthy region and applied safe fallbacks to keep requests working while we restore capacity.”
  - Reassurance: “Your data and requests are unaffected; we prioritize preserving correctness for critical flows.”
  - Actionable: “If you need consistent low-latency for a specific customer segment, we can pin their routes to Dedicated capacity or enable regional pinning.”

- During remediation (30–120 mins):
  - Explain tradeoff: “To keep throughput up we temporarily use shorter generation limits and a faster model variant that preserves answer quality for X% of typical prompts. This reduces cost and latency while we bring capacity back.”
  - Tell customers what to expect: “You may see slightly shorter completions or reduced streaming granularity; core features like intent recognition and safety filters remain on.”

- Post-incident (after stability):
  - Root cause narrative: concise timeline of events, impacted regions/models, mitigations applied (routing, variant fallback, reduced max_tokens), and follow-up actions (capacity improvements, postmortem link).
  - Recovery commitments: steps product/infra teams will take plus any changes to SLA/CDR or credits if applicable.

Canned responses (short) for support channels:
- Outbound Slack/Email (initial):
  - "We’re currently mitigating increased latency for inference in <region>. Traffic is being routed and a temporary model fallback is active to keep requests completing. We’ll share an ETA in the next 30 minutes and post a full incident summary when resolved."

- Inbound customer question:
  - Q: "Is my data exposed?" A: "No — requests and KV caches remain encrypted; routing and fallbacks occur within Redwood’s infrastructure and do not change data access controls."
  - Q: "When will full behavior return?" A: "We’re targeting restoration within the hour; we’ll provide a recovery ETA in our next update."

Talking points for AEs and SEs (more technical but customer-friendly):
- Why Redwood’s fallbacks are safe:
  - We use model-variant compatibility rules: fallbacks preserve tokenization and safety layers, and are validated by automated eval suites for each model family.
  - Prefix/KV cache continuity: cached context is preserved across compatible variants to avoid regressions in chat state.
- Multi-region behavior in plain English:
  - Smart routing moves new requests to healthy regions while minimizing cross-region data transfer. For customers with regional data constraints, we surface regional pinning options (Dedicated or Private deployments).
- Graceful degradation knobs customers can control:
  - max_tokens limit, sampling/temperature adjustments, disable non-essential tool-calls, enable lighter quantization profiles, and request-level priority tags for critical traffic.

Competitive analysis notes (how to position against common competitors):
- Competitor A (hosted-first, single-region fallback):
  - Weakness: global failover often results in wholesale model substitution without cache continuity -> customer experiences context loss and unpredictable output changes.
  - Redwood angle: emphasize continuity (KV/prefix cache preservation) and controlled variant compatibility to keep stateful apps working.
- Competitor B (self-host/on-prem heavy):
  - Weakness: customers must build their own fallback routing and testing; operational burden high.
  - Redwood angle: we provide built-in, tested fallbacks and visibility (rollout dashboards, canary/fallback toggles) with optional Private deployments for regulated workloads.
- Competitor C (low-latency edge claims):
  - Weakness: edge-only focus lacks unified rollout and fallback policies across regions; inconsistent SLOs across customers.
  - Redwood angle: unified runtime and routing policies across hosted, dedicated, private so customers get predictable SLAs and escalation paths.

Differentiators to highlight in sales motions:
- Predictable, explainable fallbacks: deterministic variant selection rules and pre-validated compatibility sets reduce surprise model regressions.
- Observability: per-route latency/cost breakdowns and real-time tracing means customers see what changed (not just that something changed).
- Business controls: pinning, traffic-prioritization, and dedicated regional pools for customers who need guaranteed latency.
- Automated safety-preserving degradation: safety layers (filters, policy enforcement, and eval hooks) remain active even with faster variants.

Incident narrative template (for postmortem summaries) — keep to one page:
- Title + brief impact statement (1–2 lines): what customers saw and scope.
- Timeline (eg. T+0, T+15, T+45): actions taken (traffic routing, model fallback, capacity scale-up), and customer-facing messages sent.
- Root cause: evidence-based cause and contributing factors.
- Mitigation and recovery: what we did to restore full experience.
- Follow-ups: short-term fixes, long-term improvements, and owners + ETA.
- Customer outreach plan: recommended RACI for accounts > $X M ARR.

Language do's and don'ts (trust-focused):
- DO: Use active, concrete verbs and time-bound commitments ("We have routed traffic and expect restoration by 16:45 PST.").
- DO: Explain impact in terms of customer functionality rather than internal metrics ("Completions may be shorter" vs "p50 tokens increased").
- DON'T: Use absolutes without qualification (avoid "never"/"always").
- DON'T: Overpromise SLA adjustments; route those requests to Pricing/Legal after product/infra confirm remedies.

Quick checklist for customer-facing owners (pre-incident prep):
- Ensure account’s routing/pinning preferences are captured on the customer record.
- Know which customers have Dedicated or Private (and their contact playbooks).
- Have canned email/Slack templates in a shared doc with placeholders.
- Keep an up-to-date list of impacted routes/models and their fallbacks.

Open questions / tradeoffs we’re tracking (for GTM + product sync):
- How granular should public incident language be about model variants to balance transparency vs. confusion?
- Should we offer a templated customer SLA credit commitment for availability incidents above X%? (finance/legal input needed)
- How to surface fallback behavior and costs in Console without overloading standard customers?

Immediate next steps (recommended):
- Finalize 3 short Slack/email templates for first-contact, mid-incident, and post-incident updates (owner: Priya).
- Add a small FAQ card to the hosted-api docs that explains fallback semantics in plain language (owner: Diego).
- Run tabletop with top 10 accounts to rehearse conversations and capture pushback (owner: AE leads).

Notes to self / drafty bits:
- Include a line about billing protection if an incident leads to elevated retry rates — follow up with finance.
- Consider a one-page "why fallbacks matter" infographic for SDRs and AE playbooks.

Reference snippets and resources:
- Internal availability playbook: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/GT/availability-playbook
- Incident classification rubric (SRE): ENG-4123
- Recent fallback test PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/785

End of doc.
